Will these new horizontal players take over completely? Will it be winner take all? Can products that focus vertical use cases survive? The new wave of products - Muse, Town, Instinct, Grokbot, etc - come from taking the power and magic of Openclaw/Hermes but wrapping it in polished, secure, consumer-friendly experience. This is only the beginning, and soon every major tech company will throw their hat in the ring and thousands of startups that have been working on vertical agents in X (travel, shopping, family, work, SMB, etc etc) have big existential questions to answer.

The simple case against winner-take-all dynamics: These agents are tools, not networks. They inherently provide a solo experience, and although packaged as chat experiences, they don’t have network effects the way that Whatsapp or phone networks do. They’re more like email clients - I can use Superhuman and someone else uses Outlook and someone else is on Gmail, but in the end we just send email to each other. In that metaphoi, if a Muse agent encounters a Instinct agent, they will just figure out how to talk to each other by building APIs, or using email/messaging/etc., so that there’s no advantage to everyone running the same thing. Further, you can swap out the underlying LLM - as we saw in the Claude vs Clawdbot saga - things will still work. The memory and underlying context are just text files, and AI are great at porting things from one system to another. So where’s the moat?

Just because they are tools today doesn’t mean they can’t evolve into networks. As I’ve written about in the past, instead of discussing “network effects” as a vague/amorphous concept, let’s instead overlay it against core KPIs each product has to build against:

- Acquisition network effects: More users** = lower CAC, higher virality, more signups
- Engagement effects: More users = higher retention, deeper usage, more frequency
- Monetization effects: More users = higher ARPU, higher conversion, more share of wallet
(**PS. and by “more users” of course I actually mean, of course, higher network density with more interconnection within/across networks. Not scale effects)

So looking at these sub-categories of network effects, you might ask: What are the features that you’d build to actually create network effects in agents? How does this category become winner-take-all?

Acquisition:
In the pre-AI world, network effects in customer acquisition were driven by users taking actions that then bring in even more users - whether that’s sending an invite, sharing a piece of content, or getting mentioned in a comment. Those users would then join the network, repeat the same actions, creating more viral loops that would throw off more users. In the post-AI world, both users and agents can initiate these loops. An agent might suggest, “hey, do you want me to help organize a New Years celebration with family” and then might pull together a group chat with your siblings, in-laws, and parents. It might build a microsite for the event and ask people to sign up and RSVP, creating an opportunity to generate a signup. Or for work, you might finish a slide deck and your agent asks if you want to pull together a meeting to present it to your team. When it does that, it might create a prep doc, take notes, and host it all on a microsite that engaged others.

These types of agentic viral loops need a few things to work: They need to be able to plug into your contacts, and to have enough context to know when to loop which people into which projects/events/activities. They need access to communication channels like email/messaging/otherwise, specifically where they can reach potential users, as this serves as the viral substrate for propagation. The magic will be how to get all of these things without being creepy, and to create enough trust to reach out to friends/colleagues/etc on your behalf, without being too push. No one wants an agent that says, “hey Andrew would like to get lunch next week” followed by “and sign up for this agent to agree!” - it has to be better and more subtle than that.

Many viral loops in the pre-AI era, particularly in the workplace, were built on a content creation loop - you use Google Slides to make a thing, you share a link, and then people would view it. Eventually they might make their own. Many products like Figma, spreadsheets, Notion, Canvas, are all built on this loop, and so are YouTube, Instagram, etc. In the agentic world, you might start by talking to your agent about interior decoration ideas, and it might ultimately build you a Pinterest-like board and make it easily shareable with others. It might build you a spreadsheet mini-app with a budget, a schedule, etc., and again, make it easily shareable. It might volunteer to do this inside a group chat with your friends, and if they want to view it, they should sign up and get their own agent too.

If the content creation loop works for agentic virality, I think it means there’s a big incentive for every agent to volunteer to make visually-appealing, shareable content, do this often. AI is so good at codegen that creating a one-off disposable artifact will probably be more useful than not. And there’s a big incentive to drive virality by building/owning the content yourself as the agent. In the interior decoration example, it would be more viral to create a standalone version hosted by the agent, rather than building an actual Pinterest board, or to build a self-contained mini-spreadsheet rather than creating a GSheet. A properly tuned agentic viral loop will do the former because it helps spread the agent, rather than helping spread Pinterest/GSheets.

This might all sound like horrific spamminess to you, but I think it might be done tastefully. If an agent is high-retention and high-usage, you’ll have many shots on goal to gradually invite your friends onto the same platform as you. The first shot might come from an invite loop that says your colleague/friend wants to set up a place to share photos/coordinate calendars/etc., and even if you say no, over time, your friend might share very useful microsites for projects or events or research that’s relevant, and you might decide that you want to sign up to leave a comment, but then eventually you might try the other functionality as well.

🏀 14 wins in 16 mock drafts. Only TWO builds managed to beat OG.

Last week, I ran the 5-Day OG Mock Draft Challenge on Facebook. The challenge was simple:
Draft from different positions across a 14-team, 9-CAT league using the FantasyBoysOG Draft App and see whether OG could consistently construct a #1 projected roster — regardless of where I was picking.

Across 16 mock drafts:
🔥 14 finished #1.
Only two teams managed to beat my builds:
⚡ SGA Punt-AST Build
The familiar, go-to SGA construction — sacrifice assists and lean hard into everything SGA naturally gives you.
🧪 Tyrese Triple-Punt Build
This was the one that really caught my attention.
And these weren't blowouts.
In both cases, my OG build finished only around 0.5–3 points behind.
The matchups:
🏀 Pick #7 — Tatum build
vs. SGA Punt-AST
🏀 Pick #13 — Durant + KAT build
vs. Tyrese Triple-Punt

But the triple-punt build is the one I've been thinking about.
In H2H 9-CAT, you don't need to be good at everything.
You need to win 5 categories.
So what if you deliberately stop trying to compete in three categories?
Instead of spreading roster value across all nine, you sacrifice three and build overwhelming strength across the remaining six.
In theory, you're building toward a very repeatable:
5–4 / 6–3 winning path.
But there's a trade-off.
If you've deliberately removed three paths to victory, your margin for error inside the remaining six becomes much smaller.
One injury.
One bad schedule week.
One opponent whose strengths happen to overlap with yours.
And suddenly that supposedly secure 5–4 becomes much less secure.

So I'm curious what experienced 9-CAT managers think:
Would you actually commit to a TRIPLE PUNT for an entire season?
Can that level of specialization consistently get you through the regular season and into the playoffs?
And once you're there...
Would you trust it in a one-week playoff matchup?
👇 TRIPLE PUNT: legitimate championship strategy or too fragile?

👀 Want to see the complete lineups behind these two teams — and the other OG #1 builds from the Mock Draft Challenge?

Follow FantasyBoysOG .

I'm opening access to the OG Web App, where you can dig deeper into the builds, rankings, category profiles and roster analysis behind the challenge.
🏀 Same game. Higher insights.

Benim de yapmak istediğim bir proje vardı. Yazdım ve hemen onaylandı.

Anthropic tarafında:
• 12 ay Claude Team (aylık $625'a kadar indirim)
• $1.000 API kredisi
• Anthropic ekibiyle birebir görüşme hakkı

Üstüne Claude Startup Stack ile diğer araçlarda toplam $45 bine varan teklifler geliyor. Benim en beğendiklerim:
• ElevenLabs: 12 ay ücretsiz + 33 milyon karakter
• Linear: 6 ay ücretsiz Business
• Granola: 3 ay ücretsiz Business
• Hex: 6 ay ücretsiz Enterprise
• Lovable: yıllık Business planında 4 ay indirim
• Gamma: Pro yıllıkta ilk yıl %25 indirim

Claude projemi zaten biliyordu, başvuru formunu da Claude'a doldurttum. Bu kadar hızlı onay geldiği için muhtemelen karşı tarafta da Claude onayladı.
Yani Claude bana Claude kredisi kazandırmış oldu :)))

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 这两天在 X 上直接冲上趋势了，原因是真有点离谱：

1250 亿参数的大模型，稀疏 MoE 架构，每次推理只激活 60 亿参数。有人做了个叫 Strata 的一键安装包，家用游戏 PC 就能跑起来，GitHub 两天涨了 2800 多 star。

以前都说 125B 这种体量得上服务器，这条铁律算是被打破了。有实测从 25 tok/s 干到 50+ tok/s，中文圈已经有人做了硬件性价比表：Strata 加持下 Mac 全线落败，N 卡加大内存赢麻了。

本地跑等于零 API 费加数据不出门，普通人是真能动手玩了。GitHub 搜 Niko1221/Strata 就行。

text:
现在用 Claude Code 或 Codex 写代码，搭一套能跑的前端加后端可能也就一个下午。但很多人手里握着顶级工具，却天天对着空白终端发呆，不知道该写什么。

当写代码的成本降到底之后，独立开发最难的一关早就变成了怎么找到真需求。

千万别坐在电脑前硬憋什么价值百万的商业点子。凭空想出来的需求，十有八九是自嗨，写完发到社区送免费兑换码都没人领。真正在市场上能跑通的需求，全都是从别人的抱怨和笨办法里扒出来的。

分享几个平时找需求最接地气的路子：

第一个地方是小红书和闲鱼，这是国内最真实的痛点金矿。

很多写代码的人平时不刷小红书，觉得上面全是生活八卦。其实只要换个视角，去搜救命、求推荐、怎么搞、有没有懂的、干到崩溃这类词，底下全是各行各业最鲜活的痛点。

重点别光看主帖，要去翻几百条评论区。比如外贸业务员抱怨跨国单据核对太费眼、小学老师吐槽排课算分表格太难调、自媒体运营苦恼多平台排版配图太繁琐。只要评论区里有一排人在求模板、求脚本、求代处理，这就是极其强烈的信号。

紧接着拿着这个关键词去闲鱼和淘宝搜一圈。如果发现上面真有人靠人工帮别人处理这类杂活，十块钱二十块钱一单，销量还有好几百，这事就稳了。有人愿意花钱雇人手工干，说明需求早就被验证过了。别人靠人工加 Excel 苦哈哈干半小时的活，你用 AI 搓个极简网页或浏览器插件，几秒钟出结果，把原本费劲的人工服务变成随手可用的白菜价小工具，顺手再去小红书发篇解决过程，客户自己就会找上门。

第二个地方是 Reddit 的垂直行业版块，专门用来挖出海需求。

想做海外工具收美金，别去翻宏观行业报告，直接泡在 Reddit 上。除了常看的 r/SideProject 和 r/SaaS，更有价值的是去具体职业的子版块，比如独立电商卖家、房产经纪人、财务会计、播客剪辑师扎堆的地方。

直接在这些版块里搜 alternative to、too expensive、hate、manual、spreadsheet。

海外很多垂直领域的软件生态非常僵化，一套软件动辄一个月收一两百美金，界面还停留在十年前。大公司的工程师为了绩效，总喜欢往软件里堆砌无数复杂的按钮和配置项，普通用户点错两下就弹窗报错。

只要盯住那些几百万人被迫在用、但评论区天天有人骂它又贵又难用的老牌工具，这就是现成的机会。你不需要正面去抄一个全功能的替代品，只需要把它最核心的那一个功能抽出来，砍掉百分之八十花里胡哨的报表和权限设置，做成一个打开网页就能用的单点工具，价格定到原来的十分之一，就能稳稳切走一块蛋糕。

第三个地方，就是自己和身边朋友每天干活时的烦躁瞬间。

人对日常的低效特别容易麻木，每天重复几十次复制粘贴、改格式、导数据，习惯了就觉得理所应当。

平时干活时只要留个心眼，一旦觉得某个机械操作烦得让人无法忍受，同时确信写段脚本或者接个模型接口就能自动化，立马动手把它搓出来。自己用着爽，顺手丢给身边两三个同行朋友试试。如果朋友用完还会主动催你修 Bug、加小功能，这往往就是最诚实的产品起点。

找到苗头之后，立项的心态也要换一换。

不要在脑子里对自己宣布：我要做一个某某系统。人一旦下这种断言，脑子里的防御机制立刻就会跳出来吓唬自己：大厂也做怎么办、用户不留存怎么办。还没建代码仓库，自己先把项目判了死刑。

在 Vibe Coding 的时代，把每一个点子都当成一个两小时的试探问题：我能不能今晚用 AI 搓个最简原型，明天丢到小红书或 Reddit 看看有没有人搭理？

初始方案完全允许是错的。如果没人理，扔掉也只损失两个小时；一旦有人进来用、进来骂你哪里不好用，顺着用户的吐槽一路改下去，真正能赚钱的形态自然就会长出来。

text:
Zed 编辑器快到飞起的秘密，是一个叫 GPUI 的引擎，

开源了，但只有毛坯——

想拿它写应用？连个像样的按钮都得自己画🤣

结果一家券商看不下去了。

Longbridge（就是那个炒股 App 的 Longbridge）：

“我们本来就要自己造全家桶，干脆造完开源。”

于是有了 GPUI Kit，16k+ star：

✅ 75+ 生产级组件，UI 设计照着 shadcn/ui 抄作业
✅ 120 FPS，重负载下照样丝滑
✅ 20 万行不卡的代码编辑器，自带 LSP
✅ 几十万行数据的表格，虚拟滚动随便滑
✅ 神仙细节：无障碍、UI 集成测试、甚至 JS 插件运行时

而且不是实验室玩具——

Longbridge Pro 桌面客户端，第一天就跑在生产上。

一家券商，卷出了 Rust 社区最全的桌面框架，

金融圈搞开源，下手是真重啊👊👇

🔗 https://t.co/c1IhaoHNEe

text:
现在用 AI 自动做科研，最怕的其实是一处没人发现的 bug：

后面十轮实验，可能全建立在一个假结果上。

这篇 RankEvolve 研究的，就是 Auto-Research 里的「执行可靠性」。

长时 ML 实验中，Agent 很容易引入数据泄漏、漏掉归一化、断开梯度，甚至配置根本没生效。代码能跑、指标也正常，但实验已经失真。

RankEvolve 主要做了三件事：

把研究流程编译成可执行的状态机，强制 Agent 按协议推进；

让 Claude Code、Codex、OpenHands 等不同 Coding Agent 互相 review 和 repair；

保存每轮 patch、配置、指标和失败经验，避免后续重复踩坑。

在相同预算下，异构 Agent 协作把执行正确率从 45.8% 提升到 62.5%。

连续 12 轮自动研究后，在 MovieLens-20M LARGE 上，NDCG@10 比公开基线提升 4.48%。

所以 Auto-Research 跑得越久，越要先保证每一轮实验都值得相信。

否则「自我进化」很容易变成持续放大一个早期错误。

📎 arxiv: https://t.co/iRAsBrrQGX

text:
another MASSIVE idea:

it’s become glaringly obvious that personal ai agents won’t monetize users by charging $20/month.

instead they’ll monetize on the backend by taking a cut of the spend they drive to merchants.

which means every agent is eventually going to want the same thing:

discounted pricing + rev share from airlines, hotels, restaurants and every other merchant they funnel spend to.

but it makes absolutely no sense for every agent company to individually negotiate bulk pricing with thousands of merchants.

so build one network that aggregates all of the spend and:

> negotiates discounted rates  
> secures referral / rev share economics  
> wraps thousands of merchants into one API

basically a giant affiliate network for ai agents, except the purchasing power of every agent is pooled together.

this concept is nothing new either.

companies like Amex have been doing versions of this forever: aggregate huge amounts of demand, negotiate better rates and monetize the spread.

but now imagine that across every vertical of commerce and making it available to every ai agent through one API.

whoever builds this will end up sitting on a Visa-like network for agentic commerce.

quotedTweet.text:
my prediction:

personal ai agents won’t monetize through monthly subscription fees.

they’ll monetize by owning the fintech stack and earning revenue every time their users spend money.

Instinct already measures internal performance based on monthly payment volume.

to monetize this they can:

> issue their own Visa credit card
> earn 2-3% interchange on every transaction
> negotiate bulk discounts directly with merchants
> take a percentage of the savings they generate
> earn yield on balances sitting inside the ecosystem

instead of charging you $20/month to use your personal agent, the agent becomes the interface through which you spend thousands of dollars every month.

if your agent books your flights, hotels, restaurants, and everyday purchases, owning the payment layer underneath becomes far more valuable than a $20/month subscription.

the biggest personal ai companies will end up looking less like software companies and more like fintechs.

personal ai agents + fintech will eventually blend into an entirely new category: 

agentic finance.

text:
小路带你60天学系统设计Day 11/60｜CDN：把缓存铺到全球

Day 10 的缓存是"把热数据放内存里"，但有个物理极限绕不过去：用户在地球另一端，光跑一圈就要上百毫秒。内存再快，也快不过光速。

CDN（内容分发网络）干的就是这件事:把缓存铺到离用户最近的地方。

原理很直白：在全球布几千个边缘节点，把图片、视频、JS、CSS 这些静态资源缓存在那儿。用户请求不再跨洋跑到源站，而是去隔壁城市的节点拿。延迟从几百毫秒掉到几十毫秒，源站压力也卸掉了大半。

调度靠 DNS：用户一解析域名，CDN 的智能 DNS 看一眼"这人从哪来、哪个节点最闲"，就把他指过去。边缘命中直接返回；没命中就回源拉一份，顺手缓存下来，下一个人直接享用。

几个关键技术，面试常考：

缓存刷新 vs 预热：内容更新了，边缘的老缓存得清掉（purge），但 purge 传播到全球节点要时间——这就是 CDN 版的"一致性延迟"。大促前则反过来玩：提前把热点内容推到边缘，叫预热。

动态加速：CDN 不只管静态。动态请求（比如下单）缓存不了，但可以走优化链路：TCP 调优、链路复用、路由选优，让包走"高速公路"而不是"乡间小道"。

回源风暴：某个热点资源恰好全网过期，几千个节点同时回源，能把源站打爆。解法：回源合并（一个节点去拉，其他等着）、回源限流。这是 Day 10 缓存击穿的全球放大版。

Trade-off 就两个：一致性 vs 时效（purge 永远有延迟窗口），成本 vs 覆盖（节点越多、流量越大，账单越刺激）。所以小公司直接买云厂商 CDN，大厂才自建。

💡 思考题：为什么视频网站用 CDN 能省大钱，你的银行转账却走不了 CDN？（提示：想想什么能缓存、什么不能。）

Day 12 预告：负载均衡——流量来了，谁来分？

小路带你60天学系统设计 Day 10

Day 10/60｜缓存：拿内存换时间的艺术

Day 9 的一致性哈希是为缓存而生的——但缓存本身，是一整套学问。

先问为什么：数据库一秒扛几千 QPS 就喘了，RT 还得毫秒级。解法很粗暴：把热数据放内存里，读内存比读磁盘快几百倍。这就是缓存——拿内存换时间。

缓存分好几层，各管一摊：客户端缓存 → CDN → 反向代理 → 应用本地缓存 → 分布式缓存（Redis）→ 数据库。离用户越近越快，但也越难统一管理。

玩缓存就三件事：缓存什么、什么时候过期、怎么更新。

更新策略最常用的是 Cache-Aside（旁路缓存）：读时先查缓存，没有再查 DB 然后回填；写时先更新 DB，再删缓存。注意是"删"不是"更新"——删了下次读自然回填，少一次写操作，还避开了并发更新的脏数据坑。

失效靠 TTL，但 TTL 是把双刃剑。设太长，数据 stale；设太短，缓存形同虚设。

然后是三个经典事故，面试必考：

缓存穿透：查根本不存在的 key，请求全穿到 DB。解法：布隆过滤器先拦一道，或者缓存空值。
缓存击穿：某个热点 key 恰好过期，瞬间海量请求打爆 DB。解法：热点 key 永不过期（后台异步刷新），或加互斥锁只放一个请求过去。
缓存雪崩：大批 key 同一时刻过期。解法：TTL 加随机抖动，别让它们集体"自杀"；再加多级缓存兜底。
Trade-off 就一个：一致性 vs 性能。缓存越激进，性能越好，数据越可能 stale。这是 CAP 在工程里的日常版本——没有银弹，只有取舍。
💡 思考题：Cache-Aside 里为什么是"先更新 DB，再删缓存"，而不是反过来？（提示：想想删缓存和更新 DB 之间，来了个读请求会发生什么。）

Day 11 预告：CDN——把缓存铺到全球。

text:
This is how Claude Code plans should look.

It's html-plan, a plugin Thariq on the Claude Code team is testing: the plan becomes 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗯 𝗽𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝘂𝘁𝗲, and you answer its questions by clicking an option.

It opens as a tree you expand one level at a time:
→ Level 1: what users can do or see after the change, with a UI mockup
→ Level 2: how it works, with the call stack, data structures or a few lines of code
→ Level 3: the file and line it changes
Read only level 1 and you already know the whole change.

For every question, Claude has already picked the answer it recommends. Change it if you disagree, and leave a comment on any line you take issue with. Then hit Respond to get one reply. Paste it back into Claude Code, and only then does it start writing code. Any question you never opened gets flagged in that reply, and 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝘆𝗲𝘀.

The plan's text is written in ASD-STE100, the English used in aircraft maintenance manuals, which Karpathy recommended last week. Each sentence says one thing, and packing the page checks for long sentences and passive voice.

Thariq also wants it to 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲. To install:
claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community
claude plugin install html-plan@claude-community
Then type /html-plan followed by what you want to build. You'll need node.

Using Codex, or don't want to install a plugin? Add this to your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md and your plans in the terminal get written the same way 👇

## Writing plans
When I ask for a plan first, write it as a tree and wait for my reply before you start:
- Level 1: what users can do or see once it's done. One sentence per item, one line max, written as a claim that can be true or false, like "Each user can hold 50 scheduled messages at most." Don't just write "Message limit." Split by feature, not by file, module or order of steps. Reading only level 1, I should know the whole change
- Level 2: how each item works, naming the entry point, the rule or the data structure
- Level 3: where it changes, as file:line. Mark code that doesn't exist yet as a sketch
- At most 5 items under each item and at most 3 levels. Number every item, and I'll reply by number
- Put each question for me under the item it affects, 2 to 5 per plan. Give options for each and mark the one you recommend. If an option would drop an item, say which
- Write level 1 and your questions in plain language with no code names. Save code names for levels 2 and 3
- End with what you're not changing this time, then list your question numbers again
Don't take a question I didn't answer as a yes. If it matters, ask me again before you start.

This is how Claude Code plans should look.

It's html-plan, a plugin Thariq on the Claude Code team is testing: the plan becomes 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗯 𝗽𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝘂𝘁𝗲, and you answer its questions by clicking an option.

It opens as a tree you expand one level at a time:
→ Level 1: what users can do or see after the change, with a UI mockup
→ Level 2: how it works, with the call stack, data structures or a few lines of code
→ Level 3: the file and line it changes
Read only level 1 and you already know the whole change.

For every question, Claude has already picked the answer it recommends. Change it if you disagree, and leave a comment on any line you take issue with. Then hit Respond to get one reply. Paste it back into Claude Code, and only then does it start writing code. Any question you never opened gets flagged in that reply, and 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝘆𝗲𝘀.

The plan's text is written in ASD-STE100, the English used in aircraft maintenance manuals, which Karpathy recommended last week. Each sentence says one thing, and packing the page checks for long sentences and passive voice.

Thariq also wants it to 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲. To install:
claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community
claude plugin install html-plan@claude-community
Then type /html-plan followed by what you want to build. You'll need node.

Using Codex, or don't want to install a plugin? Add this to your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md and your plans in the terminal get written the same way 👇

## Writing plans
When I ask for a plan first, write it as a tree and wait for my reply before you start:
- Level 1: what users can do or see once it's done. One sentence per item, one line max, written as a claim that can be true or false, like "Each user can hold 50 scheduled messages at most." Don't just write "Message limit." Split by feature, not by file, module or order of steps. Reading only level 1, I should know the whole change
- Level 2: how each item works, naming the entry point, the rule or the data structure
- Level 3: where it changes, as file:line. Mark code that doesn't exist yet as a sketch
- At most 5 items under each item and at most 3 levels. Number every item, and I'll reply by number
- Put each question for me under the item it affects, 2 to 5 per plan. Give options for each and mark the one you recommend. If an option would drop an item, say which
- Write level 1 and your questions in plain language with no code names. Save code names for levels 2 and 3
- End with what you're not changing this time, then list your question numbers again
Don't take a question I didn't answer as a yes. If it matters, ask me again before you start.

🚨Zinedine Zidane on his conversation with Michael Olise before bringing him on against Belgium:

🗣️ Zidane: “Michael was sitting on the bench with his duvet completely covered up. I looked at him and thought, ‘Does this guy realise we’re losing 1-0 at home?’ [laughs]

I didn’t want to say anything to him at first. But at half-time, I called him over and said, ‘Michael, I want you to come on because I want you to help us win this game.’

His answer surprised me.

He looked at me and said, ‘Boss, I don’t need 90 minutes to win this game. Give me 30 or 40 minutes and I’ll win it.’

I asked him, ‘What do you mean?’

He said, ‘Look at how they’re defending. They’re compact around Dembélé and Akliouche. They’re protecting certain areas, and I already know where the spaces are. Give me the time and I’ll find a way to hurt them.’

I just looked at him and said, ‘Okay. Let’s see.’

At around the 60th minute, I called him and said, ‘Michael, it’s time.’

He looked at me and said, ‘Coach, don’t worry. I don’t need a warm-up. I’m already warm.’

He stood up and walked straight to the touchline.

The funny thing is, I didn’t even have many instructions for him. I just wanted him to go and play his football.

As he was coming on, Ousmane Dembélé came off and handed him the captain’s armband. I heard Ousmane say to him, ‘Go and win this game.’

And from the moment Michael stepped onto the pitch, I could feel something had changed.

Suddenly Belgium were dropping deeper. They were turning. They were running towards their own goal instead of ours.

Seventeen minutes later, Doué scored.

Four minutes after that, Cherki made it 2-1.

Then Michael scored.

Two minutes later, he scored again.

I was standing there scratching my head thinking, ‘This kid actually told me he was going to win the game.’

That’s the part I love about Michael. It wasn’t arrogance. He had already watched the game for 60 minutes from the bench and understood exactly where the spaces were.

He didn’t come on hoping the game would change.

He came on knowing how he was going to change it.”

text:
The most common reasons why AI pilots fail, even at the 'best' companies:

In order of prevalence:

1. Not starting with a thorough process mapping exercise (standard operating procedures vs. what’s actually happening across systems)

2. Automating a process step instead of the entire process (saving 8 mins in a 22-day process still leaves you with a 22-day process)

3. Not capturing baseline metrics for cycle time, cost per transaction, error rate, etc.

4. Building a sidekick instead of a background agent (chatbots will always only be used by ~10% of users)

5. Not embedding the AI into the organization’s existing systems of record (if users have to login, adoption will be low)

6. Not assigning an AI owner (IT built it, the business tolerated it, and no one was “on call” when it broke)

7. Not engaging legal, infosec, and finance early (we routinely see pilots “discover” these groups in month 3 - and get immediately killed)

8. Not scoping for exceptions (the “demo” only covers the “happy path” - but exceptions often represent 40%+ of process volume)

9. Not running the AI in “shadow mode” for a period of time to build confidence (going straight to production often leads to an AI mishap in front of the CFO)

10. Building with only a single AI model provider (one price hike or deprecation later, the pilot is a migration project)

11. Focusing on vanity metrics (e.g. # of logins, “adoption”) instead of business metrics (time saved, $ generated, risk reduced)

12. Not planning for month 7 (who will own and pay for the AI?)

13. Not engaging the subject matter experts (if you capture all their knowledge in an AI, what incentive do they have to help?)

🚨Breaking: Anthropic engineers revealed a simple trick they use internally.

Claude agents can now remember how to improve themselves.

A file called:

AGENT_LEARNINGS.md

The AI updates this file whenever it makes a mistake.

Inside it:

• mistakes it made
• patterns to avoid
• better approaches

Before starting new tasks, the agent reads the file.

Result?

The agent gets smarter over time without retraining the model.

This is called external memory scaffolding.

Expect this pattern to show up in every serious AI agent system.

♻️ Repost to share with your audience.
✔️ You can follow @swadeshkumar_ for more internal updates.

User simulation may become one of the most important and underappreciated parts of agentic RL.

We spend enormous compute making agents better, then often evaluate them against static tasks or scripted users. A realistic user simulator could make long-horizon training, personalization, and product testing much more useful.

The real test for Kairos is not just whether it sounds human. Given a person's history, can it predict their held-out choices in unfamiliar situations? And can it recognize when it does not have enough evidence?

Otherwise, we may end up with population stereotypes wearing a personalized voice.

Very interesting direction, @kevinbanghe.

quotedTweet.text:
Today we introduce Kairos 1: the world's first model built to simulate individual human behavior. Frontier models only understand population averages, ignoring the individual differences that make us human.

Kairos beats Persimmon, Astra, Fable, and Gemini across 13 simulation benchmarks.

text:
I stopped asking AI to find bugs. I've built an AI workflow that runs semi-automatically and consistently finds Critical issues.

I used this system alone in the @immunefi audit competition for @QuantusNetwork. It found a Critical issue nobody else did, and I finished 2nd out of 98 researchers.

Then, with two days left in the @Firelightfi Audit Competition, I ran it and found a paid High.

Same for the ENS Audit Comp. I launched it in the last two days and found me a Critical.

Honestly, I’m very proud of this AI workflow I've built. And I'm still improving it to work for Bug Bounties even more autonomously.

I already knew the system worked because it constantly finds issues in private client repos. But seeing it work in a public contest, with everyone looking at the same code, is different.

And yes, I genuinely need to start doing bug bounties.

I wrote an article explaining exactly how I did it, which models I used, what worked, and also what failed.

Btw, screenshot with proof below.
